newsitem.title: USA: Albright said to prod rethink on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Albright said to prod rethink on Zaire.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, unhappy with options offered her regarding Zaire, directed U.S. experts to rethink plans to help resolve the central African crisis, officials said on Wednesday.
Officials told Reuters this does not necessarily mean the United States will reverse its opposition to a U.N.-French proposal for a multi-national force to intervene in Zaire.
But the issue remains under discussion by the adminstration and with allies, the officials said.

Albright, who took office in January, has devoted considerable time to the deteriorating situation in Zaire. According to officials, at a recent senior staff meeting, she expressed disatisfaction with the planning and options available for her and President Bill Clinton to consider.

"When an issue strikes her as not being handled well by the interagency process -- like Zaire -- she calls a meeting in her offices ... and says we're behind the curve," one official said in an interview.
"She forced everyone to think anew about the problem and ratcheted up the pressure ... We're moving towards newer positions and more thought-through positions on Zaire."

He said questions she posed included: "What if there is a ceasefire agreement? Are we ready to work on a peace implementation force? What if there is no ceasefire agreement and there is chaos in the country? What is our position then?"
Another official said: "The secretary asked the (State) department to think anew about ways we can do more ... She hasn't been happy with the options we have."
"I think the secretary wants to be pro-active. She's trying to look for some way so that we're not being accused of not doing enough" in Zaire, he added.

French President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday denounced a "conspiracy of silence" on Zaire and pressed the world to force a ceasefire there. On Wednesday, Paris urged European Union allies to help mount a humanitarian airlift for refugees. There were anti-U.S. protests in Kinshasa.

Ugandan-backed rebels fighting the government of autocratic French-backed President Mobutu Sese Seko have captured a swathe of eastern Zaire, driving Rwandan Hutu refugees before them, and threaten the key garrison city of Kisangani on the Zaire river.
Rebel leader Laurent-Desire Kabila accepted a U.N. peace plan, strongly promoted by South Africa and the United States, as a basis for peace talks but rejected its ceasefire call.
Albright, like many others in the international community, is concerned the civil war could dismember Zaire with violence spilling across borders into neighbouring states.

U.S. policymakers "are going to have to start looking hard. How can we stop this conflict from spreading? Nobody has taken a position to do anything at this point. The secretary wants to see if there is more we can do," one official said.
"France and others have said the United States is standing in the way of doing something about Zaire. We are trying to do things. We're just not wanting to do what they are trying to do," he said.

Some officials say Paris is keen to draw Washington into the conflict to stabilise the situation so Mobutu can stay in power. But one official said: "We honestly don't care whether he stays in power or not. We're not siding with either side."

For the moment, the United States, whose participation is considered key, remains adamantly opposed to a multi-national force. "Frankly, we're not convinced at this point that a multi-national force would serve a useful purpose," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Wednesday.

But he was defensive against criticism of the U.S. role, saying: "We're doing the right things. But there is a crisis and there's a political crisis, it's a rebel offensive. We can't control the situation." REUTER 122327 GMT mar 97
